claims.text: Ti40Zr40W10Mo10 is a dual-phase refractory high-entropy alloy.
The untreated as-cast alloy has relatively coarse grains, limited grain-boundary density, and minimal deformation twinning.
Hot rolling will eliminate defects and refine the grains of Ti40Zr40W10Mo10.
Rapid annealing after hot rolling will stabilize a fine-scale dual-phase structure containing nanoscale precipitates and twins.
The proposed processing will produce a refined, homogeneous dual-phase microstructure with a higher density of deformation twins.
Deformation twins accommodate plastic strain and thereby make deformation more uniform.
Rolling followed by partial or rapid recrystallization can retain processing-induced twins and yield a favorable strength-ductility combination.
Stabilizing the refined dual-phase and precipitate structure will preserve or enhance high strength.
Phase stability is responsible for preserving impact-induced energetic release after thermomechanical processing.
The treated alloy will have higher fracture strain or plastic elongation than the as-cast baseline.
The treated alloy will exhibit improved uniform deformability relative to the as-cast baseline.
The ductility improvement will occur without a significant loss of high strength.
The thermomechanically treated alloy will retain impact-induced rapid energy-release capacity.
Ti40Zr40W10Mo10 can sustain approximately 2300 MPa compressive strength at a strain rate of 3000 s^-1 and can exhibit deflagration during dynamic deformation.
The proposed treatment will be effective under both quasi-static and approximately 3000 s^-1 dynamic loading at room temperature.
The untreated alloy's lower ductility and non-uniform dynamic deformation are caused by coarse grains and limited twin formation.
The hypothesis may generalize to refractory HEAs having similar dual-phase compositions and microstructures.
The hypothesis may not apply to single-phase HEAs.
Excessive precipitate coarsening or aggregation can degrade dynamic mechanical properties.
A fracture-strain increase of at least 20% relative to an as-cast control is the proposed benchmark for a successful ductility improvement.
